chapter_title: Structs, Custom Types, and Arrays of Structs

screens.title: Structs, Custom Types, and Arrays of Structs
screens.subtitle: Group related data, create readable types, and build dynamic collections with self-referential structs.

narration.text: In this chapter you will learn how to group related pieces of data into single, meaningful units using C's struct construct. We'll begin with the idea that a struct is simply a blueprint: it describes what fields a complex value will have, but it does not yet create any storage. You will see how to declare a struct, create variables from it, and access fields with the dot operator. Then we'll use typedef to make those types feel like built-in names and show how arrays of structs let you manage collections of those values. After that, you'll explore pointers to structs and the arrow operator, learn why dynamic allocation is necessary when you need flexible sizes, and finally build a simple singly linked list using a self-referential struct. Each step includes concrete code examples and a short pitfall check so you know what to avoid, like confusing dot and arrow or forgetting to free memory. By the end you'll be able to design small record types, store many of them, and connect them dynamically.

keyIdea.title: Why structs matter
keyIdea.text: Structs let you model real-world entities by grouping different fields under one type, making code clearer and safer than parallel arrays.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Structs & Arrays
Structs, Custom Types, and Arrays of Structs
From blueprints to dynamic lists: how grouping fields turns scattered variables into clear, maintainable code.

You will see how a struct describes a compound value, how typedef makes that description easy to use, and how pointers and dynamic memory let you build flexible collections like linked lists.

This reduces errors from parallel arrays and makes passing related data to functions simple and expressive.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part 1
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this section

narration.text: By the end of this first objectives slide you will be able to define custom compound types, access their fields, and begin organizing collections of those types. First, you will learn to define a struct using the struct keyword so you can group heterogenous fields like strings, integers, and floats into a single logical entity. This matters because it keeps related data together and simplifies function interfaces. Second, you'll practice accessing members with the dot operator; that gives you a clear and direct way to read and write fields of a struct variable. Third, you'll learn how typedef creates a concise alias for a struct type, which makes subsequent declarations less verbose and easier to read. Fourth, you'll create arrays whose elements are entire struct values, so you can manage many records with familiar indexed access. Each objective will include a short example and a small mnemonic to help you remember which operator or keyword to use. Think about a student record as a concrete example: grouping name, id, and gpa into one variable is immediately more robust than parallel arrays.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part 2
screens.subtitle: Pointers, dynamic memory, and linked lists

narration.text: In this second objectives slide we'll focus on pointers, dynamic allocation, and building a simple linked list. First, you will learn how to declare and use pointers to structs; pointers let functions manipulate large records without copying and enable dynamic structures. Second, you'll practice the arrow operator, which is shorthand that dereferences a struct pointer and accesses a member in one concise expression. Third, you'll use malloc and free to allocate and release memory for structs at runtime; safe code checks the allocation result and frees memory when it is no longer needed. Finally, you'll build a basic singly linked list using a self-referential struct where each node contains data and a pointer to the next node. This skill ties together pointers and structs and introduces common mistakes such as forgetting to set next correctly or leaving dangling pointers after free. Each objective includes a short example so you can try inserting nodes and freeing a list safely.

screens.title: What is a struct?
screens.subtitle: A lightweight blueprint that groups related fields into a single type

narration.text: A struct is a user-defined composite type that groups variables of different types under a single name. Think of it as a recipe card or a student ID card: instead of keeping a separate name string, id number, and numeric field scattered across the program, a struct bundles them into one cohesive value. The declaration describes the fields and their types; it does not allocate storage. For example, declaring a Student struct tells the compiler each student value will have a name array, an integer id, and a float gpa. This makes code safer and easier to reason about because related data travels together. A common misconception is to think a struct declaration itself creates variables or memory — it does not. You still must declare variables of the struct type to allocate space. As a concrete example, after defining struct Student you can declare struct Student s1; and then set s1. id or copy a name into s1. name. Takeaway: structs model real entities, reduce parameter lists when passing related fields to functions, and improve code organization. Ask yourself: what related fields in your next program should be bundled into a struct?

keyIdea.title: Struct = blueprint
keyIdea.text: Declaration defines the shape; variables of that struct type allocate storage and hold grouped fields.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › What is a struct?
Definition
A struct is a user-defined data type that groups variables of different types under a single name. It describes the layout of a compound value and is used to model related pieces of information as one unit.
Analogy
Imagine a recipe card: it lists all fields required for one recipe. A struct is that card in code and each declared variable is one printed card you can use.
Key takeaway
Declaration does not allocate memory. You must declare variables of the struct type to store actual values.
Example declaration
// Define a Student type
struct Student {
  char name[50];
  int id;
  float gpa;
};

// Declare a variable of that type
struct Student s1;  // allocates storage for one Student
Explanation: the struct block tells the compiler the fields and types. The later declaration s1 reserves memory for that layout.

screens.title: Declare and initialize struct variables
screens.subtitle: How to set up instances and populate fields safely

narration.text: After you define a struct type, you create variables of that type and populate their fields. In C, you can declare a variable using either the full tagged name like struct Student s; or, later when we introduce typedef, you can use the alias. To copy strings into a fixed array member, use a string copy routine instead of direct assignment because arrays are not directly assignable. You can also use an initializer list when declaring a variable to set all fields at once — this is compact and useful for literals. A common error is attempting to assign one array to another with the equals operator; that will not copy the characters. As a concrete example from the chapter, after declaring struct Student you might call a string copy to put "Alice" into the name array, set the id integer, and assign a float to gpa. When initializing with braces, ensure the field order matches the declaration. Takeaway: use string-copy functions for array members and prefer initializer lists for concise known values. Question to consider: if a name might be longer than the array, what safety checks should you add before copying?

keyIdea.title: Initialize with care
keyIdea.text: Use initializer lists for whole-value initialization and string-copy functions for fixed char arrays; never assign arrays with =.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Declare & Initialize
Code example
#include <string.h> // for strcpy

struct Student {
  char name[50];
  int id;
  float gpa;
};

int main(void)
{
  struct Student s1;
  strcpy(s1.name, "Alice");
  s1.id = 12345;
  s1.gpa = 3.8f;

  // initializer list
  struct Student s2 = {"Bob", 54321, 3.5f};

  return 0;
}
Explanation
  • Use strcpy to place a C-string into a char array member.
  • Use s.field to set or read members on a struct variable.
  • Initializer lists set fields in declaration order.
Common mistake
Attempting to assign a char array directly with the equals operator will not copy characters; use a copy function instead.
Key Takeaway

Treat struct variables as single values and use dot syntax and initializer lists to set fields correctly.

screens.title: Using typedef with structs
screens.subtitle: Make struct types concise and readable

narration.text: Typedef creates a new name for an existing type. When used with structs it removes repetitive 'struct' keywords from later declarations and makes your types feel built-in. There are two common patterns: create an anonymous struct and typedef it directly to a name, or give the struct a tag name and then typedef that tag to a shorter alias. Both approaches result in a simpler declaration syntax. For example, using typedef you can write Student s1; instead of struct Student s1;. This reduces visual noise and improves readability, especially when your struct is used frequently. A pitfall to avoid is confusing the tag name and the alias; they are different tokens. Another practical question: when should you choose an anonymous struct with typedef versus a tagged struct? Use a tagged struct if you need to refer to the struct type in pointer declarations inside the struct itself, such as when making self-referential nodes. The key takeaway: typedef improves ergonomics but be intentional about naming so code remains clear. Using typedef with structs means use typedef to give structs concise names so declarations read like built-in types; prefer tagged structs for self-references.. In practical terms, make struct types concise and readable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Typedef for clarity
keyIdea.text: Use typedef to give structs concise names so declarations read like built-in types; prefer tagged structs for self-references.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › typedef & Aliases
Before and after
// With a tag name
typedef struct StudentTag {
  char name[50];
  int id;
  float gpa;
} Student;

// Now you can write:
Student s1;

// Or anonymous struct with typedef
typedef struct {
  char name[50];
  int id;
  float gpa;
} StudentAnon;
When to use a tag
If the struct needs to refer to itself via pointers (self-referential), use a tag name so the type name is available inside the definition.
Example: benefit
Using an alias shortens later declarations and makes code that manipulates many struct variables much easier to read.
Pro tip

Prefer clear alias names and keep the typedef close to the struct definition so the association is obvious.

screens.title: Arrays of structs and memory layout
screens.subtitle: How arrays store multiple struct instances and how to access them

narration.text: Arrays of structs let you manage many records using familiar indexed access. When you declare an array whose element type is a struct, each element holds a full instance of that struct. The array's memory is contiguous: element zero occupies the first block, element one the next block, and so on. That makes indexed access efficient and predictable. As a concrete example, declaring Student class_roster[100]; reserves space for 100 Student values in a row. You then access members with class_roster[0]. id or copy a name into class_roster[1]. name. A common confusion is thinking the array holds pointers to structs — it holds full structs unless you specifically declare an array of pointers. If you need variable-length collections or dynamic growth, you will instead allocate arrays dynamically or use linked lists. Remember also that copying a struct assigns all fields; assigning one array element to another copies the whole record. Takeaway: arrays of structs are ideal for fixed-size collections with fast indexed access; choose pointers if you need flexible sizing or polymorphic behavior. Arrays of structs and memory layout means an array of structs stores full instances back-to-back; indexing plus the dot operator lets you access any field quickly.. In practical terms, how arrays store multiple struct instances and how to access them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Array = contiguous struct instances
keyIdea.text: An array of structs stores full instances back-to-back; indexing plus the dot operator lets you access any field quickly.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Arrays of Structs
Example: array of structs
// Declare an array of 100 Students
Student class_roster[100];

// Set fields of the first element
strcpy(class_roster[0].name, "Charlie");
class_roster[0].id = 98765;
class_roster[0].gpa = 3.7f;

// Copying elements assigns all fields
class_roster[1] = class_roster[0];
Memory layout
Elements are stored contiguously; element i is at base + i * sizeof(element).
Common misconception
An array declared as Student arr[10] stores full Student values, not pointers. Declare Student *arr[] when you want pointers.
Key Takeaway

Choose arrays for fixed-size needs with fast indexing; choose dynamic allocation or linked lists for variable sizes.

screens.title: Pointers to structs and the arrow operator
screens.subtitle: When to use -> versus . and how pointers change access patterns

narration.text: Pointers to structs are essential when you want to avoid copying large values or when you need dynamic structures. If you have a pointer variable that stores the address of a struct, dereference it to access members. In C the arrow operator is a convenient shorthand: instead of writing open parenthesis asterisk pointer close parenthesis dot field, you write pointer arrow field. Both forms are equivalent, but the arrow is cleaner and common. For example, if you have a Point p1 and Point *ptr_p1 = &p1;, then ptr_p1->x and (*ptr_p1). x yield the same value. Pointers also allow you to pass large structs to functions without copying them, offering performance benefit and enabling in-place updates. A frequent mistake is using dot on a pointer variable; dot requires a struct value, not a pointer. The practical rule: use dot for direct struct variables and arrow for struct pointers. Consider also pointer lifetimes: ensure the pointer points to valid storage before dereferencing, and do not dereference after freeing. Pointers to structs and the arrow operator means the arrow operator combines dereference and member access; use it when you hold a pointer to a struct.. In practical terms, when to use -> versus . and how pointers change access patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: -> = dereference + access
keyIdea.text: The arrow operator combines dereference and member access; use it when you hold a pointer to a struct.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Pointers & Arrow
Pointer example
typedef struct {
  int x;
  int y;
} Point;

Point p1;
Point *ptr_p1 = &p1;

// two equivalent forms:
(*ptr_p1).x = 10;
ptr_p1->y = 20;
Explanation: arrow is shorthand for dereference then dot access, and it reads more naturally for pointers.
When to use pointers
Pass large structs to functions, share mutable state, or build linked structures with next pointers.
Common mistake
Using the dot operator on a pointer variable is incorrect; dot operates on a value, not on a pointer.
Check your understanding

Is the pointer pointing to stack storage or heap storage? Confirm before dereferencing to avoid undefined behavior.

screens.title: Dynamically allocating structs
screens.subtitle: Use malloc and free to control struct lifetimes

narration.text: Dynamic allocation gives you control over when struct storage is created and released. Using malloc you request a block of memory large enough to hold the struct and receive a pointer to it. Always check the returned pointer for NULL before using it. When finished with the struct, call free to return the memory to the system and avoid leaks. The chapter shows allocating a Point on the heap, assigning its fields, printing them, and then freeing the pointer. A common error is forgetting to free allocated memory, which causes memory leaks over time, or freeing memory too early and later dereferencing a dangling pointer. Another mistake is casting the result of malloc in C unnecessarily; follow your project's style. As an example practice, allocate a dynamic Point, set coordinates, print them using the print function, and then free the pointer and set it to NULL to prevent accidental reuse. Takeaway: dynamic allocation enables flexible data structures, but it requires disciplined allocation checks and frees. Dynamically allocating structs means use malloc to create struct storage at runtime and free to release it. always check for failure and null out pointers after freeing.. In practical terms, use malloc and free to control struct lifetimes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Allocate and free
keyIdea.text: Use malloc to create struct storage at runtime and free to release it. Always check for failure and null out pointers after freeing.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Malloc & Free
Heap allocation example
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <stdio.h>

typedef struct {
  int x;
  int y;
} Point;

int main(void)
{
  Point *dynamic_point = (Point *) malloc(sizeof(Point));
  if (dynamic_point == NULL)
  {
    printf("Memory allocation failed!
");
    return 1;
  }
  dynamic_point->x = 100;
  dynamic_point->y = 200;
  printf("Dynamic point: (%d, %d)
", dynamic_point->x, dynamic_point->y);
  free(dynamic_point);
  dynamic_point = NULL;
  return 0;
}
Allocation checklist
  • Call malloc with sizeof(type).
  • Check the returned pointer for NULL.
  • free when finished and set pointer to NULL.
Common mistake
Failing to free allocated structs leads to memory leaks; freeing too early leads to dangling pointer use.
Key Takeaway

Heap allocation enables variable-sized structures but requires explicit lifecycle management.

screens.title: Self-referential structs and linked lists
screens.subtitle: Nodes, next pointers, and the head of a list

narration.text: A self-referential struct contains a pointer to the same struct type, which is the essential building block of a linked list node. The chapter shows a Node struct that stores an integer and a pointer to the next Node. The list is tracked by a head pointer that points to the first node or is NULL when the list is empty. To insert at the head, you allocate a new node, set its data, set its next pointer to the current head, and return the new node as the new head. This pattern lets you grow the list quickly with constant-time head insertions. A common misconception is that linked lists are always superior to arrays; they have different trade-offs: linked lists excel at insertions and removals when you don't need random access, while arrays provide fast indexed reads and contiguous memory locality. Example code in the chapter demonstrates insert_at_head, print_list, and free_list functions. Key takeaway: a correctly managed head pointer and careful next assignments keep the list intact and avoid broken links. Self-referential structs and linked lists means a node holds data and a pointer to the next node; the head pointer identifies the list start and null marks the end.. In practical terms, nodes, next pointers, and the head of a list. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Node + next = linked list
keyIdea.text: A node holds data and a pointer to the next node; the head pointer identifies the list start and NULL marks the end.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Linked Lists
Node definition and insert_at_head
typedef struct Node {
  int data;
  struct Node *next;
} Node;

Node *insert_at_head(Node *head, int value)
{
  Node *new_node = (Node *) malloc(sizeof(Node));
  if (new_node == NULL) exit(1);
  new_node->data = value;
  new_node->next = head;
  return new_node;
}
Explanation
The new node points to the previous head, and the returned node becomes the new head. If head was NULL, the new node's next is NULL and it is the only element.
Pitfall
Failing to set new_node->next correctly will sever part of the list. Always assign next before returning.
Key Takeaway

Linked lists use self-referential structs; insertion at head is simple and efficient but requires careful pointer updates.

screens.title: Printing and freeing a linked list
screens.subtitle: Walk the list, print values, and release memory safely

narration.text: Traversing a linked list requires iterating node by node, following the next pointers until you reach NULL. The chapter shows a print_list function that starts at head, visits each node, prints its data, and moves to the next node. When freeing the list, save the next pointer before freeing the current node so you don't lose the link to the remainder. Freeing everything is essential to avoid memory leaks. The provided free_list function loops, stores current->next, frees current, and then continues with the saved pointer. A common mistake is freeing current and then trying to access current->next; that leads to undefined behavior because the freed memory may no longer be valid. Also, after freeing the entire list, set the head pointer variable in the caller to NULL if you intend to reuse it. As a concrete exercise, try building a list with three values using insert_at_head, print it to see the order, then free it and confirm there are no remaining allocated nodes. What would you change to insert at the end instead of at the head? Printing and freeing a linked list means always save the next pointer before freeing the current node, and set freed pointers to null when appropriate.. In practical terms, walk the list, print values, and release memory safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Traverse & free safely
keyIdea.text: Always save the next pointer before freeing the current node, and set freed pointers to NULL when appropriate.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Print & Free
print_list and free_list
void print_list(Node *head)
{
  Node *current = head;
  while (current != NULL)
  {
    printf("%d -> ", current->data);
    current = current->next;
  }
  printf("NULL
");
}

void free_list(Node *head)
{
  Node *current = head;
  while (current != NULL)
  {
    Node *next_node = current->next;
    free(current);
    current = next_node;
  }
}
Key steps
When freeing, always save the pointer to the next node before calling free on the current node.
Bug pattern
Accessing current after free or forgetting to set next correctly will cause crashes or memory corruption.
Try this

Modify insert_at_head to create an insert_at_end function that appends nodes and handles the empty-list case.

screens.title: Arrays vs. linked lists
screens.subtitle: Choosing the right representation for collections

narration.text: Arrays and linked lists are two common ways to store collections of values, and each has trade-offs. Arrays provide contiguous storage, which gives you O(1) indexed access and predictable memory locality for performance. However, arrays have fixed capacity when declared statically, or require reallocation when resized dynamically. Linked lists use nodes that point to the next node, so insertion and removal at the head or near known nodes are constant time operations and do not require shifting memory. The cost is slower indexed access because you must traverse nodes to reach an element and additional memory for pointers. Use arrays when you need fast random access and predictable memory, and use linked lists when your primary operations are frequent insertions and deletions and you want flexible growth without large reallocations. A common misconception is that linked lists always save memory; in practice pointers add overhead and fragmentation may increase overall memory use. Consider your performance profile and memory constraints before choosing. Arrays vs. linked lists means pick arrays for fast random access and locality, and linked lists for flexible insertion and deletion without moving blocks of memory.. In practical terms, choosing the right representation for collections. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Trade-offs matter
keyIdea.text: Pick arrays for fast random access and locality, and linked lists for flexible insertion and deletion without moving blocks of memory.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Arrays vs Linked Lists
Arrays of Structs
  • Contiguous memory layout with predictable indexing.
  • Fast random access via indices (O(1)).
  • Fixed-size unless you allocate dynamically and resize.
Linked Lists (Nodes)
  • Dynamic growth without moving existing nodes.
  • Fast insertion/removal at head or known positions.
  • Slower random access and extra memory for pointers.
When to use arrays
Fixed-size rosters, where indexed reads are common.
When to use lists
Queues or stacks implemented with frequent insertions and removals.
Memory note
Pointers add overhead; measure if memory is tight.

screens.title: Design choices and common pitfalls
screens.subtitle: Naming, initialization, pointer safety, and memory hygiene

narration.text: Good struct-based design uses clear names, consistent initialization, and disciplined memory handling. Prefer meaningful type names through typedef so your declarations are expressive. Initialize struct variables where possible, and set pointer members to NULL when they have no target to document intent. When allocating memory, always check for allocation failure and handle it gracefully. Free every allocation when it is no longer needed to avoid leaks, and set freed pointers to NULL to reduce the risk of accidental reuse. Be careful updating next pointers in linked lists; a single incorrect assignment can lose the rest of the list. Another common issue is confusing arrays of structs with arrays of pointers — both have different performance and memory characteristics. As a concrete practical rule: write small helper functions such as insert_at_head, print_list, and free_list to centralize pointer logic and reduce bugs. Final question to reflect on: which helper functions would you write to make your own record type easy and safe to use? Design choices and common pitfalls means name types clearly, initialize fields, check allocations, and centralize pointer updates to reduce bugs and memory errors.. In practical terms, naming, initialization, pointer safety, and memory hygiene. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Make safety habitual
keyIdea.text: Name types clearly, initialize fields, check allocations, and centralize pointer updates to reduce bugs and memory errors.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Best Practices
Naming & typedef
Use typedef for concise names, keep the typedef close to the struct, and choose names that reveal intent.
Initialization
Initialize struct variables and set pointer members to NULL if they do not yet point to valid storage.
Memory hygiene
Check malloc results, free when done, and avoid using freed pointers by setting them to NULL.
Centralize pointer logic
Write small helper functions for insertions, deletions, printing, and freeing so pointer updates are implemented in one place and easier to test.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three essential ideas from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the most important points to take forward. First, a struct groups related fields into a single user-defined type. It provides a clear way to model real-world records and reduces the complexity of passing many related values to functions. Second, choose access and storage patterns intentionally: use the dot operator on struct variables, use the arrow operator on pointers to structs, use arrays of structs for fixed-indexed collections, and use dynamic allocation or linked lists for flexible growth. Third, practice safe memory and pointer handling: check allocations, free memory when done, set pointers to NULL after freeing, and centralize pointer updates in helper functions. These three ideas—modeling with structs, correct member access, and disciplined memory management—are the core of the chapter and will let you design safe, readable C programs that manage complex data cleanly.

keyIdea.title: Three pillars
keyIdea.text: Struct modeling, correct access patterns, and careful memory management form the foundation for building reliable C data structures.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Key Concepts
struct
A user-defined type that groups different fields into one named record.
. and -> operators
Use dot for struct variables and arrow for pointers to structs; they are not interchangeable.
Arrays & Lists
Arrays store contiguous struct instances for fast indexing; linked lists use nodes and pointers for flexible growth.
Final Takeaway

Model related data with structs, choose the right storage for your needs, and handle pointers and memory deliberately to avoid common bugs.

narration.text: Keep these quick references handy as you code. First, typedef shortens struct names so Student looks like a built-in type. Second, when building lists, remember head points to the first node and the last node's next is NULL. Third, always free dynamically allocated memory and avoid using pointers after free. These three reminders will help prevent the most common errors you will encounter when working with structs and dynamic structures. When stuck, trace pointers on paper, check allocations, and centralize pointer updates into small, testable functions.
